source.title: ReDeEP: Detecting Hallucination in Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Mechanistic Interpretability
source.authors: ZhongXiang Sun; Xiaoxue Zang; Kai Zheng; Yang Song; Jun Xu; Xiao Zhang; Wei-Jie Yu; Han Li

page_placements.theme: Copy-suppression and copying heads in the competition between in-context text and stored facts

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses copy-suppression heads as a possible explanation for losing information retrieved by Copying Heads, but does not identify or test copy-suppression heads or any of the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: Appendix C speculates that copy-suppression heads might suppress information retrieved by Copying Heads; this is not tested. The paper's own RAG results measure related Copying Head and context-use behavior, not the proposed GPT-2 L10H7 suppression behavior. The cited Copy Suppression study's results are not this paper's results.
record.test_reason: The paper studies RAG hallucinations in Llama models via Copying Heads and Knowledge FFNs. It mentions copy suppression heads only in Appendix C as a speculative explanation: "may be due to the presence of some Copy suppression heads". It never identifies, ablates or measures any copy-suppression head, nor GPT-2 L10H7, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that RAG hallucinations arise mainly from the LLM losing information retrieved by Copying Heads, plus Knowledge FFNs over-adding parametric knowledge. They speculate, untested, that copy suppression heads may cause that loss.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes RAG hallucinations in Llama models using context-use scores, FFN scores, and interventions; it does not reproduce the GPT-2 small L10H7 copy-suppression analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: In Llama2-7B-chat on RAGTruth, 1006/1024 heads had higher ECS on truthful responses. Attended spans were judged correct in 77.5% of hallucination cases, implying attended information is lost downstream. The authors speculate copy suppression heads cause this loss, but do not test it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In RAG, hallucinations often occur despite correct attention to context, through downstream loss of copied information. The cause is unidentified; copy suppression is only hypothesised.

fits_no_version.finding: Copying Head scores correlate with hallucination-related ECS patterns (PCC 0.41 and 0.46). Noising Copying Heads raises NLL more than noising matched control heads.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Llama RAG settings, OV-identified Copying Heads contribute causally to context use and truthfulness.

record.problems: The paper does not directly test copy-suppression heads; the proposed connection is speculative. The reported NLL intervention comparison is only shown in a figure, without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The attended-span evaluation relies on GPT-4-o judgments.
record.rows_left_out: Detection benchmark scores, AARF truthfulness comparisons, and FFN-only results were left out because they do not measure the copy-suppression behavior in the claim.

untested.parts: All: GPT-2 small L10H7 and its suppression role across the training distribution.
All: the QK/OV mechanism and the 76.9% loss explanation.
All: calibration effect of copy suppression.
All: copy suppression as a self-repair mechanism.
All: no negative or copy-suppression heads are identified in Llama or in other tasks. Appendix C only hypothesises their presence.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification is right, and all rows correctly link to 'none'. The only contact with the claim is one speculative sentence in Appendix C citing McDougall et al. 2023. That sentence is not a result on any version.

versions.untested_parts: GPT-2 small L10H7, suppression of tokens predicted by earlier components and present in context, and whether this is its main role across the training distribution.
The head's QK/OV circuits implementing copy suppression and explaining 76.9% of its effect on loss.
Whether copy suppression improves calibration by reducing overconfidence in naive copying.
Whether ablating an upstream copier induces self-repair partly through reduced copy suppression.
Whether negative heads in narrow tasks or other models and sizes perform the same copy-suppression role.
The distribution-wide share of self-repair attributable to copy suppression versus other mechanisms.
